blogs.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
blogs.description: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is…
blogs.content:
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:

 Luna [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.

 — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

blogs.description: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just…
blogs.content:
GitHub Octoverse 2026

I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

 This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

 The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this:

 Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]

 Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]

 Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

 Tags: github , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , disclosures , agentic-engineering

blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
blogs.description: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a…
blogs.content:
I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games .

 Tree Appreciator

 Emberwick

 Battle Drones

 Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove

 Four times as insulting

 What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

 You should build a game!

 Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

 3D modeling

 Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox )

 Game design (!)

 That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play .

 Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.

 Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did .

 In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing.

 I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.

 I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

 Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

 Tree Appreciator

 The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code.

 I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

 Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

 I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

 This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it.

 It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

 Emberwick

 This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

 Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening

 Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great

 Here's that first version . It worked really well!

 I was inspired to increase my ambitions:

 Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that

 Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village

 Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll

 Here's that version .

 When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:

 Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good

 We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.

 Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.

 Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.

 There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.

 Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave".

 Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.

 I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well.

 Battle Drones

 This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.

 This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is.

 The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play.

 I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up .

 Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules.

 It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna :

 Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game .

 I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!

 Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove

 I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.

 I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.

 I called it "Quarter Sun Cove".

 I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.

 Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.

 It's absurdly cute.

 You can play the latest version here . I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.

 Here's the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file . Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.

 I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.

 This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times.

 Four times as insulting

 If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once .

 I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself.

 The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.

 We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck!

 Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!

 I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction!

 I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.

 What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

 The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input . The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).

 Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and...

Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,193 new readers. Last year, Genie 3 let you wander an AI-generated world for a few minutes. Genie 4 lets you talk to the ‘people’ living in the simulation.
 Google DeepMind’s newest world model brings its own soundtrack too, and a demo of a humanoid robot playing checkers inside one of its worlds shows where Google wants to take things next.
 Reminder: Our next live workshop is today at 2 PM EDT — join and learn why AI deep research has gotten worse over the past six months, and how to get sharp, decision-ready reports out of it again.   RSVP here .

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Genie 4 brings sound and interactivity to AI worlds

 Anthropic starts developing its own drugs

 Make editable product mockups with GPT-6.1 Terra

 Axiom’s AI swarm checks math’s longest proof

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 GOOGLE DEEPMIND
 🧞  Genie 4 brings sound and interactivity to AI worlds
 Image Source: Google DeepMind

 The Rundown: Google DeepMind just introduced Genie 4, its next-gen world model that turns prompts into explorable, photorealistic scenes in real time, with features like built-in, natively generated audio and lifelike people that users can actually interact with.
 The details:
 Genie 4 is the first Genie model to generate its own sound, like background noise and music, with characters in the worlds also now able to hold live conversations.

 Users move with keyboard controls and can use text prompts to create changes mid-scene, with the scene staying coherent between inputs.

 A simulated Apptronik Apollo robot played checkers in one demo, with Gemini 4 Argon planning each move in a nod to Genie’s future robot-training applications.

 The model debuts in research preview for trusted testers, with Google’s AI Ultra subscribers and Gemini API partners getting access next.

 Why it matters: Genie’s progress has been pretty wild to watch, and this iteration’s jump, with sound and characters you can actually talk to, takes it somewhere new. The gaming applications are obvious, but Genie is starting to look as much like a full-blown director’s tool as a world simulator.

 TOGETHER WITH CUBE
 🧠  The semantic layer for AI

 The Rundown: Cube is the semantic layer for AI. Every agent gets the same governed answer from your metric definitions and access rules. Ask the hardest questions, get real answers.
 With Cube, you can:
 Connect Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery

 Let AI build and maintain your data model

 See how Brex reached nearly 90% answer relevance

 Try Cube free (no card needed) .

 ANTHROPIC
 💊  Anthropic starts developing its own drugs
 Image source: Anthropic

 The Rundown: Anthropic shared early results with its drug-development partners and revealed it’s now running its own drug discovery programs, including buying Mithril Medicine, a solo-founder biotech whose Claude-assisted muscular dystrophy candidate could reach human trials as early as late 2028.
 The details:
 The candidate showed promise in mice within 18 months, with Claude helping solo founder Cody Tranbarger juggle contracts and tests at 11 outside labs.

 Tranbarger also turned out to be “Professor Oak,” a biotech account run pseudonymously on X for six years, and calls the setup a “Pipeline-in-a-Person.”

 At Enveda, Claude wrote a first draft of a key regulatory filing in 4 hours vs. ~3 months by hand, and also flagged seven batch-record issues humans missed.

 In another case, three of roughly 35K antibodies Claude designed for Divergence Labs appeared to beat today’s main drug at unhooking allergy triggers from cells.

 This week’s IPO filing pitched a global pharma market expected to top $2T this year, but Anthropic warned its own drug bets “may never generate revenue.”

 Why it matters: Dario Amodei said in August to expect “early glimmers” from Anthropic’s biology push in the coming months, and we’re seeing the groundwork for that. With Anthropic also running its own wet lab, and its IPO filing saying Claude can operate gear like microscopes, the pieces for AI’s hands-on science are falling into place fast.

 AI TRAINING
 📦   Make editable product mockups with GPT-6.1 Terra

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use the new GPT-6.1 Terra to build a product mockup in Blender. You’ll create two color options and a wide campaign image, then save the scene so you can handle client changes without starting over.
 Step-by-step:
 Save an empty Blender project and connect Terra through ChatGPT Work’s Computer Use plugin. Keep its access limited to your practice project

 Give Terra the guide’s carton dimensions and colors. Check the size, then add the product name and label as editable text

 Add a camera and studio lights, then render a small preview. Check that the lettering is readable, the edges look right, and the carton sits on the ground

 Copy the scene to make a second color option. Create a wide version with the product on the right and space for a headline on the left

 Export all three images and reopen the saved Blender file. Check the image sizes and confirm you can still change the text and product colors

 Pro tip: Keep the camera and lights fixed when comparing colors. Otherwise, a lighting change can make one option seem better for the wrong reason.

 PRESENTED BY SCRIBE
 🔍   Consultants take months. Scribe takes days .

 The Rundown: Most orgs map workflows the slow way: outside teams, interviews, and months of workshops. Scribe Optimize maps how work happens across your org automatically.
 With Scribe Optimize, you can:
 Map real workflows — no surveys or consultants

 Surface inefficiencies leadership can’t currently see

 Build your AI strategy on ground truth, not gut feel

 See what's actually happening in your org .

 AI & MATH
 🧮  Axiom’s AI swarm checks math’s longest proof
 Image source: Axiom

 The Rundown: AI math startup Axiom completed a fully machine-checked version of math’s longest-ever proof, called the ‘Classification of Finite Simple Groups’, with its team steering an AI agent swarm that rebuilt the decades-long effort in 24 days.
 The details:
 The theorem catalogs what Axiom calls the “periodic table of symmetry,” a full list of the basic pieces that every symmetry pattern in math breaks down into.

 100+ mathematicians spread the original across roughly 15K pages and 500+ papers, and Axiom says no single expert has read it cover to cover.

 Axiom broke the work into 108 milestones, then dozens of agents produced ~43M lines of Lean, the coding language that lets a computer verify each logical step.

 The theorem stands, but AI caught a false claim in one key step, then patched it with a new proof based on 1976 work by mathematician Ronald Solomon.

 Why it matters: OpenAI used agents to crack the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem in September, and now a startup has pointed one at a 15K-page proof that no mathematician could check alone. Dario Amodei’s “country of geniuses in a datacenter” feels like it’s coming to life in the sciences, and a lot more progress is coming with it.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Anuradha built a one-person sales team with Claude
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Anuradha :
 “I use Claude, connected live to Airtable through MCP, as a one-person GTM team. It runs a daily pipeline war room, drafts outreach, and helps me create data-driven LinkedIn content.
 I start a morning war room session by opening Claude and letting it read my live Airtable pipeline. It gives me a scoreboard of what moved, what is stuck, and who needs a touch that day. It drafts outreach using a written style rulebook: peer tone, hypothesis framing, short sentences, and no brochure language. I review everything and send it myself.
 I log every LinkedIn post in Airtable with its full text, followed by its analytics: impressions, industry mix, seniority, comments, and notes on what worked. Before writing a new post, Claude reviews the full post history, ranks the posts, and identifies which patterns drove reach and engagement from my target audience. What makes this work is that the analytics live in the same table as the content, so every post makes the next one smarter.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

 📰  Everything else in AI today

 U.S. President Donald Trump   posted that he will be “BANNING the term, ‘AI/Artificial Intelligence,’ in all relevant documents” in another push towards Super Intelligence.

blogs.name: Stratechery
blogs.title: Meta Earnings, Muse and the Frontier, Musebook
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.
blogs.content:
Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

I joined Myke Hurley on the Cortex Podcast to discuss how I write Stratechery. Then, I joined John Collison on Cheeky Pint to ( again ) interview United CEO Scott Kirby . Both podcasts were recorded a couple of weeks ago but just posted in the last few days.

On to the Update:

Meta Earnings

From Bloomberg :

Meta Platforms Inc. shares fell after Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg told investors the company would bet even more aggressively on artificial intelligence. During its quarterly earnings report Wednesday, the social-media giant boosted its capital spending plans for the year and announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses. The moves show that Meta has confidence that its already-stratospheric spending on AI is bearing fruit. After struggling to persuade investors to accept ballooning costs, Meta has made headway with its technology in recent months, especially with a new AI agent called Muse. Zuckerberg pointed to that progress as reason to keep plowing ahead.

Meta is indeed plowing ahead; from the Wall Street Journal earlier this week:

Meta Platforms unveiled a plan to raise up to $95 billion in waves of stock offerings, as the company embarks on a cash-raising spree to fund its massive investments in artificial-intelligence infrastructure. The Facebook parent said Monday it will launch roughly $35 billion in public offerings, comprising $22.5 billion of Class A common stock and $12.5 billion of depositary shares representing mandatory convertible preferred stock.

Meta also plans to establish an at-the-market stock offering program of up to $60 billion, potentially beginning in the first quarter of 2027. That is the program by which the company will create a new class of nonvoting stock, a move it previously announced. The company expects to sell shares of its new “Class C” stock over time, though Meta said Monday it hasn’t finalized the arrangement.

One year ago, after Meta’s 3Q 2025 earnings, I wrote that the company was realizing the true cost of Reality Labs :

What I also think is happening is that Meta is finally paying the price for the billions of dollars it has spent on Reality Labs with precious little financial return to show for it. Yes, investors have long grumbled at how much money Meta has spent on AR and VR, but ultimately I think Zuckerberg has gotten a pass; even the stock market freakout in 2022 was more about TikTok and ATT than about the Metaverse (the Metaverse spending was taken as an indication that Meta’s core business was faltering).

This time, however, Zuckerberg once again seems to be asking for a blank check, and given that the last blank check is growing, not cashing, I think that investors are hesitant about writing another one. Again, I’m not sure this is necessarily fair — Meta is clearly leveraging more compute effectively in its ad business, and AI is not the Metaverse — but unless Zuckerberg wants to become the world’s biggest ad business salesman he’s going to need to show some tangible evidence sooner or later that Meta can in fact win on product.

What a difference a year makes. Meta has indeed shown up asking for that blank check, and just for context, this now-$97.5 billion worth of equity offerings very nearly matches all of Reality Labs’ recorded losses. Now, to be fair, those recorded losses only go back to Q4 2019; Meta bought Oculus for $2 billion in 2014, which is to say the cumulative losses since then are higher than the $100.8 billion on the books. Still, the fact we are in the same ballpark points to how much larger the AI expenditures are in aggregate.

What is different is that I strongly believe that Meta has earned the benefit of the doubt, and not just because I have been on the record since 2024 that Meta had arguably the largest AI opportunity ; rather, go back to what Zuckerberg wrote in July 2025 when Meta’s AI efforts seemed dead in the water, even as the company was spending millions of dollars on talent and making billions of dollars worth of compute commitments:

As profound as the abundance produced by AI may one day be, an even more meaningful impact on our lives will likely come from everyone having a personal superintelligence that helps you achieve your goals, create what you want to see in the world, experience any adventure, be a better friend to those you care about, and grow to become the person you aspire to be. Meta’s vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We believe in putting this power in people’s hands to direct it towards what they value in their own lives.

This is distinct from others in the industry who believe superintelligence should be directed centrally towards automating all valuable work, and then humanity will live on a dole of its output. At Meta, we believe that people pursuing their individual aspirations is how we have always made progress expanding prosperity, science, health, and culture. This will be increasingly important in the future as well. The intersection of technology and how people live is Meta’s focus, and this will only become more important in the future. If trends continue, then you’d expect people to spend less time in productivity software, and more time creating and connecting. Personal superintelligence that knows us deeply, understands our goals, and can help us achieve them will be by far the most useful.

It is difficult to overstate how important Muse is, not just in terms of what it represents in terms of AI , or the business opportunities , but specifically that it represents Zuckerberg delivering on his promise in a way that Reality Labs has never come close to doing. Yes, investors are grumbling about Meta’s spending plans and this equity raise, which is reasonable given that dilution is, as I noted yesterday , forcing existing shareholders to pay up. If Muse didn’t exist, however, and if it didn’t hew so closely to exactly what Zuckerberg promised he would build, I think there would be a revolt by the stock market.

---

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: every Substack creator is also a Stripe customer, and that’s the case for many other creator platforms.

Of course, they didn’t succeed because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

Muse and the Frontier

From Artificial Analysis on X :

Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets.

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New benchmarks are, in my estimation, the only benchmarks worth paying attention to, because by virtue of being new, models have not been bench-maxxed, i.e. trained specifically to do well on the benchmarks in question. To that end, here is the Index :

The rankings here roughly match my sense of the landscape and, for what it is worth, my experience:

Opus 5.5 is the best model, although the GPT-6 family is very strong.

Chinese models are really not that close to the frontier (although Kimi K3.1 Pro’s showing is impressive; it’s also the largest Chinese model by far). This is obvious when you use them (which is to say that using them makes you very aware of what bench-maxxing means in practice).

Google and Meta are very much on the frontier, albeit not state-of-the-art (Grok, meanwhile, is falling far behind).

Meta’s comeback here is notable, and necessary: for all of the product sensibility that goes into Muse, it really does feel like the model is just barely good enough, which makes sense when you see Muse Spark Open’s score on this chart; you also realize why the release of Muse Wonder was an important milestone, and what a difference it is going to make when Meta figures out how to serve it efficiently to more users. Zuckerberg said on the earnings call :

And then there’s just continuing to increase the value in the product which I think we will largely do by continuing to develop new models. That’s why I mentioned that we launched Muse first on Muse Spark, and that’s what is currently the default across the free tier. And we rolled out Muse Wonder, and people can access that in the paid tier today. And we know that it performs a lot better, so we’re working on getting a more efficient version of Muse Wonder that we’ll be able to roll out more broadly. But you can imagine just as we iterate forward in two, three models into the future, when you have significantly higher intelligence and capability to solve many more problems for people and the ability to deliver that at a much more affordable price point, I think that that’s going to just unlock a lot more value to people. So we’re very excited about that.

Muse presents to investors a very binary question: if you think that it is a tremendous opportunity, then you must support Meta’s compute spending, because spending is the only way to get better models. That was, as I noted yesterday , the most important takeaway from Anthropic’s S-1: R&D compute is massively larger than inference compute, and its share of the total compute bill is growing. Yes, serving Muse will cost a lot; making Muse great will, at least for a while, cost more.

This also, I must admit, gave me more sympathy for Meta’s enterprise aspirations. The project is, to be clear, entirely solipsistic ; Zuckerberg said as much in his opening remarks:

One other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high-margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise Platform, led by CJ Desai. Muse Wonder and even more advanced models that we are training can serve additional high-margin services beyond the Muse network, including our API, Muse Code, and other enterprise services.

What I mean by solipsistic is that the enterprise initiative is coming into being not because enterprise customers are asking for it, but because Zuckerberg sees the need to maximize the number of call options on the massive training costs he’s incurring. What makes me more sympathetic is that it is more likely than I thought that there will be enough inference compute to go around if this effort hits (just because the share of compute going to inference is likely lower than I originally thought). If I’m honest, I still think it’s an unnecessary distraction, but sometimes solipsism is self-preservation!

That noted, the most compelling argument for investors opposed to this spending is not that Muse doesn’t need it, but that Meta actually doesn’t need Muse. CFO Susan Li started out her summary of the company’s business results thusly:

Q3 Total Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, up 26%. Q3 Family of Apps ad revenue was $63.1 billion, up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis. In Q3, the tota...

blogs.title: Anthropic S-1, The Cost of Compute, Who Is Paying?
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Anthropic's IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution.
blogs.content:
Anthropic's IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech — also available on video on YouTube and Spotify — Andrew and I discussed Netflix, security, and our experience with Meta’s VR glasses; then on Sunday’s subscriber-only mailbag we covered Ubiquiti, the Tim Cook era in retrospect, and Y2K.

On to the Update:

Anthropic S-1

From Bloomberg :

Anthropic PBC filed for its long-awaited IPO, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead. The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing Monday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

The filing moves Anthropic a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced AI models to go public. Anthropic and some of its shareholders are offering stock in the IPO, according to the filing. The amount of shares they’re offering will be disclosed in a later filing.

Anthropic’s IPO will serve as a litmus test for how much investor demand exists for new equity tied to the AI trade, after optimism surrounding the technology helped power a four-year bull market in US stocks. Just two hours before Anthropic’s filing, Meta Platforms Inc. said it is seeking to raise as much as $95 billion from selling common and preferred stock in one of the largest equity offerings in history. Earlier this year, Google-parent Alphabet Inc. targeted raising as much as $85 billion in equity. Anthropic is expected to be followed onto public markets next year by its main competitor, OpenAI.

Numbers, finally — albeit somewhat incomplete ones. The figures provided are through June 30, i.e. the end of Anthropic’s major growth spurt; those numbers go stale on November 12 and will have to be updated if Anthropic doesn’t list by then — current expectations are the week of November 16.

Anthropic has in many respects timed this listing perfectly, thanks to the explosion in its top-line revenue in the first half of this year which, combined with the company’s delay in securing compute, led to extremely impressive margins (more on these in a moment); it will be interesting if somewhat slower growth in the 3rd quarter puts a damper on the listing (or possibly a revelation that Opus 5.5 re-accelerated growth turbocharges it). Revenue growth is, needless to say, a very big deal.

The Cost of Compute

The most interesting financial numbers were absolutely buried in the S-1 , all the way down on F-39 in the “Consolidated Financial Statements”; that is where Anthropic actually broke out its costs by function:

The two most interesting are Cost of Revenue and Research and Development, because that is where the company’s compute costs lie (along with Sales and Marketing, which is where the cost of free access is housed). Those still aren’t entirely clear numbers, particularly because Research and Development contains personnel costs, but you can make some assumptions to get to the following estimate (I subtracted the Cost of Revenue and estimated free inference — I used half of Sales & Marketing — from total compute to come up with R&D compute):

There are some really interesting takeaways here.

This is a real tech company , in that Anthropic has meaningful leverage on its cost to serve. In the first half of this year the company had gross margins of 85%.

Gross margins are inflated because Anthropic reports gross revenue from access to its models sold through AWS, Azure, and Google; those costs are in Sales and Marketing, and may be somewhere around 37% on around half their revenue. Still, these are real tech company margins, at least once revenue is big enough.

Anthropic’s compute costs are dominated by R&D. Moreover, the cost of R&D compute is increasing faster than the cost of inference, at least over the last year.

What this means is that Anthropic in isolation seems like an incredible business; the challenge, however — and one reason why the company might want the industry to “pace the frontier” — is that the cost of R&D compute is the variable that is arguably the most out of their control. The scale of Anthropic’s investment in R&D compute is a function of competition; those revenue figures ultimately rest on Anthropic having frontier models, at least for now, which means ever more compute.

This also gives a different spin to the idea of recursive self-improvement, i.e. the process where AI improves itself. Anthropic is already an RSI organism, at least from a financial perspective: the company is the biggest consumer of its own compute and its own AI, all in the service of building an even better AI. Folks complain about circular financing in the AI trade; the reality is that the companies at the core of that trade are the ultimate ouroboros, where their long-term financial upside is dependent on not eating themselves completely!

To that end, it is interesting to think about how the approximately $855 billion in future compute costs Anthropic has committed to might be allocated; the assumption is that the vast majority of that money is for inference, but if current trends hold it is R&D compute that will consume a major part of it.

---

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: every Substack creator is also a Stripe customer, and that’s the case for many other creator platforms.

Of course, they didn’t succeed because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

Who Is Paying?

That noted, the $855 billion number is an estimate — basically I added up all disclosed commitment categories, which could have some overlap — and not locked in stone:

$269.4 billion is non-cancelable minimum cloud spend with AWS, Google, and Microsoft.

$161.2 billion is non-cancelable equipment leases with Broadcom that must be paid when equipment is ready.

$21.0 billion in short-term commitments to unspecified counterparties is non-cancelable.

$85.9 billion is committed to Nscale and Lambda as capacity is accepted.

Up to $120.5 billion in commitment to SpaceXAI is cancelable with 90 days notice starting in 2027.

The remaining ~$200 billion is a catch-all for unknown commitments.

The hyperscaler angle is particularly interesting. First, those are the contracts that are the most concrete. Second, those contracts were, in the case of Amazon and Google (and Broadcom), signed in conjunction with Note Purchase Agreements (NPAs), in which the hyperscalers basically loan money to Anthropic with the right to convert that debt into equity. That money, of course, flows right back to the hyperscalers to rent compute.

So who is actually paying? Despite those incredible margins, Anthropic reported an $80 billion loss in the first half of this year, because its liability to Amazon under earlier NPAs was marked to the dramatically increasing market price of the stock Amazon was entitled to, resulting in a $72 billion fair value charge. That right there is the clue: Anthropic isn’t out extra cash because its valuation increased; rather investors were diluted.

Anthropic has $77 billion in NPAs which have not yet been drawn on, which is to say that $80 billion “loss” is only the beginning, at least if the valuation continues to increase. That money is, whenever it is borrowed for compute from the lender, ultimately paid for by investors being diluted (although there will likely never be as large of a “loss”, which is to say a corresponding gain, for those other NPAs — that was an all-time investment by Amazon); meanwhile, every time Anthropic’s valuation increases by 50%, 2% of shares may go to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund; all of this is before we get to the actual capital that Anthropic hopes to raise in this initial public offering, and the future equity offerings that will likely follow.

In short, what is happening with this IPO, along with Meta’s equity offering, which followed on Google’s offering earlier this year , is that public market investors are being asked to pay for the AI buildout that the credit market is increasingly nervous about, and those payments are not necessarily straightforward. The price isn’t just shares, but the fact those shares will inevitably represent a continually decreasing share of the company.

This is why the revenue numbers will matter. In the long run, revenue does, of course, need to cover costs; in the short run, however, revenue will matter for the narrative which public stockholders will need to buy, such that they buy assets that are set up from the beginning for dilution. That will be fine if the valuation increase outpaces the dilution, and, to be fair, it is entirely reasonable to decide stock in a frontier lab is, no matter the price, a reasonable call option on seemingly unlimited upside. That’s the thing about revenue growth: when it’s up-and-to-the-right you can get away with anything.

---

blogs.title: The End of the Internet
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it's just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.
blogs.content:
The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it's just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress.

It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install!

I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable , an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever.

The End of Blogs

2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet ; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom , also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space:

Talking Points Memo , Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000

Instapundit , Little Green Footballs , and Dooce launched in 2001

Matt Yglesias , Daily Kos , Eschaton , The Volokh Conspiracy , Power Line , Gizmodo , Gawker , paidContent , and Daring Fireball launched in 2002

Ezra Klein , Marginal Revolution , ReadWriteWeb , and AVC launched in 2003

That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference.

Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain.

Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business.

For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future :

It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost…

I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone.

In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for.

The End of Social Media

Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike the early Internet: genuinely interesting conversations happened in public, and you could reply-guy your way to broader distribution.

Social media was also free, however, and even easier to get started than a blog ever was; that meant that the amount of content was greater by many orders of magnitude. This meant that algorithms started to matter — Facebook had one relatively early, but it took Twitter much longer — and also anyone with any sort of prominence had to start taking a much more defensive approach. Community, sadly, doesn’t scale; any platform that is available to everyone starts out special and spirals from there. Ultimately, public social media sites became personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement, culminating in TikTok, a social media site with basically zero social component.

However, that doesn’t mean social networking went away: in fact, I think that social networking is stronger than ever; the difference is that it isn’t public, but is rather in group chats. Group chats are familiar, they are high trust, they are, in many respects, the best of the Internet: even as technology atomizes us the group chat is the only place you can connect with people you care about, anytime and anywhere.

In other words, the redemption of social media was — just like blogging — to become smaller. The scaling that mattered for most people was not an ever larger audience, but a proliferation of infinite finite groups. Social media 1.0 , even at its best, followed the 90-9-1 rule: one percent spoke, nine percent commented, and 90 percent lurked; the magic of group chats is not in giving everyone a voice, but a place where you feel safe to talk.

The End of the Internet

The PHP vulnerabilities were just two of a host of security issues last week alone; there were also:

Compromised intermediate CA private keys (although this was an example of sheer incompetence, not AI hacking)

Major new vulnerabilities in Node.js, GitLab, Java, and Cisco products

Breaches in LiteLLM’s supply chain and Railway developer platform

This is, believe it or not, only a partial list, and I expect things to only get worse. All of software is built on an inherently creaky human-authored foundation; the human factor meant the primary gate in all of software development was “Did it work?”, not “Is it secure from every possible privilege escalation or race condition?” or the myriad of ways that software can act in ways not intended.

The saving factor previously is that attackers were limited by human time and ingenuity as well; AI, however, has limitless time and the ability to substitute iteration for cleverness — and it’s getting pretty clever as well! It’s not a surprise that this wave of vulnerabilities is coming to light, and it’s going to get worse before it gets better — which I do, for the record, expect to happen; after all, the good guys have AI as well, and in the long run software will be better when it is (re)written by AI, and defended by agents continuously.

At the same time, what this entails is that the public Internet, to an even greater extent than now, will be a battle zone at best (i.e. social media), and a wasteland at worst (everything else). Some of this is economic, as AI consumes everything — both content and attention — without giving any of the traffic back that Google did, but it is also technical: it was already a dodgy proposition to stand up your own site or app, which was the very promise of the Internet, given the hacking risks; in the age of AI it’s madness.

It is sad. When I was a kid we called up BBS’s that were hosted in people’s homes; when I was in high school we downloaded music from public FTP addresses; when I was in college we set up our own websites. Anyone could set up a server, and that server was just as much a part of the Internet as any other server; that’s simply not viable any longer, even if you weren’t worried about making money. The Internet as we knew it is dead.

There are, however, green shoots of possibility, and once again the answer is to go smaller. When anyone can make an app, the answer is not to try and make a quick buck in the App Store; in fact, the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone. Rather, it’s to make something for yourself and a small group of trusted friends and colleagues.

This is exactly what has happened at Stratechery: we have made a bunch of different apps, for everything from podcast production to task trackers to calendar management, none of which will ever be made available publicly. That doesn’t even include the apps made for oneself: I’ve created a bunch of different apps to manage my house and sports viewing: it turns out I had a lot of software-shaped holes in my life that suddenly I can fill without asking permission.

Software has always been different from physical goods in that its zero marginal cost nature meant it could scale to far more people; at the same time, the sheer amount of up-front effort involved in creating it meant that the intended audience needed to be large enough to justify the investment. AI completely changes that: suddenly it’s possible to create software for one person, or one team; smaller target audiences aren’t just a necessity for security, they’re an entirely new and potentially much larger market for software creation at scale, by literally everyone. Or, to use the example above, the group chat era of software is here and it’s going to be so much better than what came before.
